Decisionism
deh-SIZ-hun-iz-um
noun
From Latin decidere (to decide, cut off, settle), from de- (off) + caedere (to cut) + -ism (doctrine or practice). The term arose in Reformed and conservative evangelical circles in the 20th century to critique revivalistic methods that treat a moment of human decision as constitutive of conversion, apart from sovereign regenerating grace.

Biblical Definition

Decisionism is the theological error that locates the ground and guarantee of conversion in a human decision—typically the act of walking an aisle, praying a sinner's prayer, or raising a hand at an evangelistic meeting—rather than in the sovereign, regenerating work of the Holy Spirit. In decisionist theology, conversion is an act of human will that God ratifies; in biblical theology, conversion is a work of God that includes and produces the human response of repentance and faith. The distinction is not academic; it shapes the church's evangelistic methods, its assurance of salvation, and its membership rolls. Jesus warned that many who had performed religious acts in His name would be unknown to Him on the day of judgment (Matt. 7:22–23)—not because activity is irrelevant but because activity without genuine regeneration and discipleship is no evidence of belonging to Christ. The Father draws those who come to the Son (John 6:44); no one comes by mere decision. Salvation is by grace through faith, and “this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God—not by works, so that no one can boast” (Eph. 2:8–9). Repentance and baptism as visible, public responses to the gospel (Acts 2:38) are genuine human acts, but they are the fruits of regeneration produced by the Spirit, not the mechanisms by which regeneration is initiated by human decision. Decisionism fills churches with unregenerate members who have a false assurance grounded in a moment of decision rather than an ongoing, Spirit-produced life of faith.

Origin & Era

Decisionism: the revivalistic and evangelistic error that treats a moment of human decision—a prayer, a walk forward, a raised hand—as the sufficient ground of conversion and assurance of salvation, displacing the sovereign regenerating work of the Holy Spirit.

DE-CI'SION-ISM, noun. (20th-century coinage.) The theological and methodological error of treating conversion as constituted primarily by a human act of decision, rather than by the sovereign, regenerating work of the Holy Spirit preceding and enabling that response.

Associated with the revivalist methods of Charles Finney and their wide adoption in 19th- and 20th-century American evangelicalism; Finney explicitly denied the necessity of sovereign regeneration, treating conversion as a matter of proper technique applied to human will.

Distinguished from easy believism: decisionism is broader, describing the structural assumption that a decision event produces conversion; easy believism is decisionism without the call to repentance and lordship.

Reformed critics (Iain Murray, John MacArthur) argue that decisionism produces unregenerate church membership, false assurance, and ultimately more difficult evangelism because the field is pre-occupied with people who ‘already decided.'

The confessional alternative grounds assurance in the Spirit's ongoing witness and in genuine fruits of repentance and faith, not in a moment of decision.

Key Scripture

Matthew 7:22 — "Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?"

John 6:44 — "No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day."

Ephesians 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

Acts 2:38 — "Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost."

Modern Corruption

Decisionism corrupts the church's membership, its evangelistic message, and the assurance of its members by substituting a moment of human decision for the Spirit's sovereign, regenerating work as the ground of conversion.

expand to see more

The pastoral consequences of decisionism are severe and measurable. A congregation built on decisionist evangelism will have large membership rolls and small genuine community because many members made a decision years ago and have no ongoing fruit of regeneration. When such members face assurance crises, the pastoral answer is invariably “remember the night you decided?”—which is precisely the wrong answer if the decision was not accompanied by regeneration. Conversely, genuine believers who struggle with assurance may be told their doubts indicate lack of faith, when their struggle is actually the Spirit convicting them that they need to examine whether their decision was ever genuine. Decisionism is not merely an evangelistic method; it is a theology of conversion that displaces divine sovereignty with human initiation.

The recovery is the New Testament itself: Peter's Pentecost sermon (Acts 2) produced three thousand converts not through an altar call but through a proclamation of the mighty acts of God that cut listeners to the heart; the response of repentance and baptism was commanded, received, and verified in the life of the community. The mark of genuine conversion is not a remembered moment but a persevering life of faith, increasing knowledge of Christ, genuine repentance over sin, and love for the brethren (1 John). Reformed evangelism invites people to Christ and trusts the Spirit to regenerate; it does not engineer decisions and trust the moment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin decidere (to cut off, settle) points to the moment-of-decision that decisionism makes determinative, displacing the sovereign regenerating work that alone makes any human decision spiritually real.

expand to see more

Latin de- + caedere — to cut off, settle definitively; the root of decision as a settling moment that decisionism makes the hinge of conversion

Latin decidere — to decide; in decisionism, the human decision replaces the divine decree as the operative cause of salvation

Greek metanoia — repentance, change of mind; genuine repentance is produced by the Spirit, not constituted by a decision to repent

Greek pistis — faith, trust; saving faith is the gift of God (Eph. 2:8–9), not the human contribution that secures divine response

Greek palingenesia — regeneration, new birth; the sovereign work of the Spirit that precedes and produces genuine repentance and faith (John 3:3–8)

Usage

"Iain Murray's Revival and Revivalism documents the historical shift from classic Reformed evangelism to Finney's decisionist “new measures,” arguing that the change produced a generation of nominal converts that weakened the American church."

"A useful diagnostic: after evangelistic services, does the preacher report “decisions made” or “the Spirit moved and many sought Christ”? The former language is decisionist; the latter is theologically sober."

"Churches with reformed convictions that retain decisionist methods (altar calls, counted hands) experience cognitive dissonance; consistent Reformed soteriology calls for proclamation that trusts the Spirit rather than techniques designed to produce decisions."
